EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple wildfires started during the high wind event of October 5, when humidity values dropped into the teens, and winds gusted over 70 mph in many locations in the wake of a strong cold front (see the high wind Storm Data entry from October 5). Extreme fire growth occurred, and fire fighting personnel had to fight zero visibility situations from a combination of wildfire smoke and blowing dust. Many fire fighters encountered situations where fire was burning on both sides of their vehicle. There were many occasions where the primary focus became protecting yards as the fires passed by. More than 30 agencies, including local, state, and federal, were involved in the fire fighting effort.||The largest wildfires occurred in Williams and McKenzie counties. In Williams County, there was a complex of two fires, referred to as the Ray-Tioga Fire and the Highway 85 Fire. Both of these fires crossed US Highway 2, and the Highway 85 fire nearly entered the town of Ray. Nearly 90,000 acres were burned by these fires, which resulted in two deaths and eight injuries. Approximately 425 power poles needed to be replaced as a result of the fires.||In McKenzie County there were three significant wildfires and multiple other fires, resulting in over 20,000 acres burned. The first significant fire started very early in the morning when the cold front passed through, and threatened the town of Arnegard. This fire was controlled before the strongest winds occurred. Later that morning the two main fires that developed were the Haystack Fire, which later was re-named the Elkhorn Fire, and the Bear Den Fire. The Elkhorn Fire stared 13 miles southeast of Watford City, while the Bear Den Fire occurred in far eastern McKenzie County. The Bear Den Fire threatened the community of Mandaree, on the Fort Berthold Nation, which was protected by multiple airdrops of chemical fire retardant. Approximately 200 power poles in McKenzie County had to be replaced due to impact from the fires.||In total, over 270 livestock animals died from the wildfires, and around 100 miles of fence was destroyed or severely damaged. Six cattle herds suffered health impacts from the fire and smoke. Approximately 14,000 acres of pasture and rangeland were lost, 19,000 acres of cropland suffered damage, and 1,150 hay bales burned. Two farmsteads were lost along with additional buildings, approximately 30,000 bushels of stored grain was destroyed, and farm equipment including combines and tractors were burned. Multiple vehicles were lost, and many shelterbelts and windbreaks were destroyed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There were three significant wildfires and multiple other fires in McKenzie County, resulting in over 20,000 acres burned. The first significant fire started very early in the morning when a cold front passed through, and threatened the town of Arnegard. This fire was controlled before the strongest winds occurred. Later that morning the two main fires that developed were the Haystack Fire, which later was re-named the Elkhorn Fire, and the Bear Den Fire. The Elkhorn Fire stared 13 miles southeast of Watford City, while the Bear Den Fire occurred in far eastern McKenzie County. The Bear Den Fire threatened the community of Mandaree, which was protected by multiple airdrops of chemical fire retardant. Many livestock animals died from the wildfire, and many miles of fence was destroyed or severely damaged. In addition, farm equipment was burned including combines and tractors, multiple hay bales were burned, vehicles burned, and many shelterbelts and windbreaks were destroyed. Approximately 200 power poles in McKenzie County had to be replaced as a result of the fires.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An abnormally and record dry September into the first half of October led to the ignition of the Summit Lake Wildfire which was discovered on the evening of October 18th in the northwest corner of the McCormick Wilderness between Summit Lake and Evergreen Lake. The McCormick Wilderness is located in Baraga County, 12.5 miles north of Michigamme, MI. The wildfire grew rapidly from 5 acres on the morning of the 19th to 100 acres on the morning of the 20th.  Difficult access for firefighters combined with an abundant mix of hardwood and conifer trees for fuel allowed the wildfire to expand to over 300 acres by the 27th before a combination of snow and rain on the 31st led to its eventual containment by early November.  Dozens of additional wildfires during the very warm and dry October burned over 200 acres across the U.P.  Some of the additional larger fires were the Fox Fire in northern Schoolcraft County which burned 62 acres and one structure, the Section 27 North Fire in Marquette County which burned over 28 acres, and the Round Lake Fire in Alger County that burned nearly 15 acres.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An abnormally and record dry September into the first half of October with precipitation deficits of more than 3 inches led to the ignition of the Summit Lake Wildfire which was discovered on the evening of October 18th in the northwest corner of the McCormick Wilderness between Summit Lake and Evergreen Lake. The McCormick Wilderness is located in Baraga County, 12.5 miles north of Michigamme, MI. The wildfire grew rapidly from 5 acres on the morning of the 19th to 100 acres on the morning of the 20th. Difficult access for firefighters combined with an abundant mix of hardwood and conifer trees for fuel allowed the wildfire to expand over 300 acres by the 27th before a combination of snow and rain on the 31st led to its eventual containment by early November.  Through the efforts of Ottawa National Forest personnel and resources, a Michigan Interagency Type III Incident Management Team and aircraft personnel and resources the cost of fighting the wildfire was estimated at $1.3 million.  Additional wildfires across the U.P. through the month of October resulted in about $750,000 in damages.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A vigorous shortwave trough quickly moved into portions of the Central/Southern Plains during the day on the 6th. Hazardous weather occurred on both sides of an advancing Pacific front/dryline during the afternoon and evening hours. Behind the boundary, a strong low-level jet/flow was juxtaposed atop a very dry airmass, resulting in dangerous fire weather conditions. Two large wildfires ignited during the early evening across portions of northwest Oklahoma. In the moist sector, widely scattered thunderstorm development occurred during the late afternoon. Despite strong deep-layer wind shear (as expected with a strong upper wave), limited instability proved hostile for sustained severe convection/outcomes. A transient supercell thunderstorm moved across southern portions of the Oklahoma City metro area, producing isolated wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The '57 Fire' spread over 5,291 acres across portions of southwest Woodward County. Two firefighters were injured, one critically.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Line fire began at 930 am September 5, 2024 at Baseline and Aplin Streets near Highland California.  High temperatures on September 5 were 107 to 112F where the fire began. The fire burned north into the Santa Ana drainage due to upslope wind flow. The wildfire grew to 36,000 acres over the next 2 weeks and was finally contained at 44,000 acres in early October. The fire was difficult to contain due to the activity in the remote and thick Bear Creek drainage. The wildfire burned a 98 year old Lookout tower on Keller Peak. The wildfire did severe damage to SR 330 including miles of guardrails and signs which was closed for repairs until November 24, 2024. The fire was contained at the ridge line at Snow Valley to Bear Mountain along SR 18.  Arson was determined to be the cause of the fire. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A good growing season through spring/summer 2023 led to decent fuel loading, compared to the previous couple of years,  before vegetation went into winter dormancy. Dormant fuels and two weeks without precipitation leading into February 26th provided a very combustible environment when combined with abnormally warm temperatures (record breaking) and high winds on Monday, February 26th.  An upper level system first brought strong winds on Monday with sustained winds peaking between 25 and 39 mph out of the west. Wind gusts peaked around 55 mph with some locations briefly gusting up to 58 to 62 mph. Not only were the winds strong but the relative humidity values also dropped to 12 to 18 percent. These conditions with the dormant and dry state of vegetation contributed to the development and spread of a few large wildfires on the 26th. Some of these fires occurred in rough terrain leading to efforts to contain the fires being of little to no gain. These fires continued through the night with little recovery in relative humidity and short lived reduced winds.              ||Going into the morning of the 27th west to southwest winds quickly increased into the 25 to 35 mph range with gusts quickly exceeding 58 mph in the late morning hours before noon. Frequent gusts of 58 to 64 mph soon picked up into the 65 to 70 mph range during the afternoon of the 27th.  Some areas saw sustained winds top out in the 40 to 45 mph range for a few hours as well. With temperatures starting out in the 50s on the morning of the 27th, afternoon temperatures were back in the 70s in no time. Despite afternoon temperatures a few degrees cooler than the day before on the 26th, relative humidity values fell into the 12 to 15 percent range. This did not help with ongoing fires and also contributed to a few new fires across the combined Panhandles, some of which merged with one another turning into megafires. The same system contributing to the high winds also pushed a cold front into the area from the north.  Fires that once were moving from west to east soon started to move from north to south behind the front. Winds behind the front continued to blow in the 25 to 35 mph range and gusting 40 to 50 mph. Communities that were initially on the right flank of the fire, out of harm's way, soon found themselves on the forward flank.||There were roughly 9 named wildfires with some of these merging into one, such as the 687 Reamer Fire which started on the 27th, the day after the Smokehouse Creek Fire started but eventually burned into and merged with the Smokehouse Creek Fire. It took until early to mid March before all fires were contained. It is estimated that at least 2,075 homes were directly impacted by the Smokehouse Creek fire and within the fire perimeter.  The fires also left residents without electricity or gas for several days after the 27th of February. A significant number of cattle and livestock were also lost, and there are cascading effects from the loss of livestock revenue. Two lives were also lost in these fires and over 4000 people were impacted. ||Texas AgriLife estimated the total economic loss to the Texas Panhandle, its economy, and the economies it feeds may ultimately exceed $1 billion from these fires. AgriLife conservatively estimated that the Panhandle suffered $123 million in agricultural and agriculture-related losses (including wildlife hunting revenue losses). The number includes $68.7 million in lost fencing, $26 million in grazing losses over 1.5 years, cattle losses of $27 million, and lost hunting revenues of $875,000 annually.

Winds gusting over 40- 50 mph pushed the fire east from Highway 207 approximately 30 miles to Highway 70 north of Pampa, Texas. The fire grew rapidly, moving at estimated speeds of six to eight miles per hour. Approximately 40,000 acres burned on February 27th, expanding to more than 900,000 acres over the next two days. EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Jenkins Creek Fire ignited on Monday, May 12, 2025, around 1PM local time. It was detected east of County Road 110 and north of County Road 16 near Jenkins Creek, approximately 15 miles southeast of Hoyt Lakes, Minnesota. It was believed to have been started by a discarded cigarette from a passing vehicle. The fire rapidly expanded due to hot temperatures, low relative humidity, and strong south winds, burning through mixed boreal forest and grassy ground cover, including areas heavily infested by spruce budworm, which contributed to the fire's intensity. The fire initially exhibited extreme behavior, including crown fires and rapid spread through dense forested areas. The presence of dead and dying trees, particularly those affected by spruce budworm infestations, provided ample fuel for the fire's growth. After a couple days, the spread slowed as crews responded, winds subsided, and moisture moved into the area. Firefighters were able to take advantage of that opportunity and built a line that held through another wind event a few days later. Since then, containment continued to be effectively established with full containment achieved on June 21st. The fire reached a maximum size of 16,490 acres.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Camp House fire began on Sunday, May 11, 2025, at approximately 2PM local time in Ault Township, about two miles northeast of Brimson, Minnesota, outside the Superior National Forest. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On this Saturday, the region sat under generally westerly upper level flow, set up between departing weak ridging to the east and another approaching shortwave disturbance moving onto the High Plains. The previous day, the 21st, a passing surface cold front had ushered  more westerly winds and a drier, continental airmass into the region. As the daytime hours passed on the 22nd, the surface pressure gradient tightened across the region, sitting between an area of low pressure and accompanying southward extending trough axis moving further east into the Dakotas and High Plains, and an area of high pressure which was slow to shift east through the Midwest. This resulted in strong south-southwesterly winds and increased mixing potential, with wind gusts of 45-55 MPH at times across portions of south central Nebraska mainly west of Highway 281.  While not an overly warm day with afternoon highs topping out in the 60s, dewpoints mainly in the 20s resulted in relative humidity values dropping into the upper teen to lower 20 percent range, especially across areas along and west of Highway 281. A wildfire started just north of the town of Riverdale around 2PM CDT, eventually burning approximately 700 acres, a home, a few outbuildings, and one fire truck before being extinguished several hours later.

Driven by south-southwesterly winds gusting over 40 MPH, this fire quickly spread, burning approximately 700 acres along a 2-3 mile path. The fire was extinguished several hours later near the intersection of 175th and Riverdale Road. No injuries were reported, but one home, a few outbuildings, and one fire department truck were lost in the fire.  At least 27 fire departments responded to assist with the fire, as well as around one dozen farmers and agricultural companies.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Another unseasonably deep upper trough moved into the western U.S. March 17th strengthening into a closed upper low over Colorado on March 18th. Strong south to southwest winds ahead of the trough resulted in blowing dust across southern Chaves County resulting in the closure of the Roswell Relief route on the southwest side of town during the afternoon of March 17th. High wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph began across the high terrain during the morning hours of March 18th moving down to lower elevations late morning as the Pacific front moved through the state. The subsidence behind the front helped to mix down strong mid and upper-level winds at the base of the newly developed low down to the surface. A strong pressure gradient was also present across the state south of a 990 mb surface low over eastern Colorado. These high wind gusts resulted in downed trees at Corrales in the Albuquerque Metro and in southwest Chaves County and blew a roof off a workshop near San Mateo in the west central mountains. The high winds also resulted in widespread blowing dust and near zero visibility across the Rio Grande Valley and eastern NM. The near zero visibility from the blowing dust resulted in multi-vehicle crashes on I-25 between Albuquerque and Santa Fe, I-40 in Torrance and Guadalupe County, and on U.S. Highway 285 south of Roswell. U.S. Highway 54 in the Carrizozo area was shut down for several hours due to the near zero visibility from the blowing dust. High winds from a shower induced microburst resulted in some power outages in east central Albuquerque during the mid evening. Winds and blowing dust subsided during the late evening hours across central and southern New Mexico, but continued across far northeast New Mexico behind a backdoor front until the late morning hours of March 19th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An unseasonably and record deep upper trough for mid-March moved through the intermountain West late on March 13th closing off into a deep upper low on March 14th. Strong south to southwest winds ahead of the trough resulted in blowing dust across southern Chaves County resulting in the closure of NM Highway 2 at Hagerman. The Pacific front moved through the state during the overnight hours of March 13th into March 14th. Subsidence behind the Pacific front combined with strong mid and upper-level winds at the base of this trough, a strong pressure gradient south and west of the newly formed upper low and 975 mb surface low across the central Great Plains resulted in widespread high wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph across central New Mexico from the early morning to around midday and across eastern New Mexico during the morning through mid afternoon hours. These wind gusts behind the Pacific front resulted in wind damage across several zones in eastern New Mexico along with widespread blowing dust across the Lower Rio Grande Valley and eastern New Mexico. Strong and dangerous westerly crosswinds even closed down I-25 from Las Vegas to Raton during the late morning to mid afternoon hours. Winds and blowing dust subsided during the late afternoon and early evening hours as the strong storm system and associated higher mid and upper-level winds, exited east of the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: High winds and elevated fire weather conditions resulted in a downed utility line on private land in Mora County east of I-25 and south of Wagon Mound that resulted in a fast moving wildfire. The wildfire prompted evacuations from two homes along a NM 271. Precipitation and lesser winds allowed crews to gain control and put out the fire by March 15th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A vigorous storm system over the central Plains, with a sub 980mb surface low over Kansas, induced a very strong pressure gradient across southeast Missouri. The result was strong south southeast winds through the afternoon and evening. Gusts 35-50 mph were common for much of the period, but the winds increased in the late evening. Perryville Regional Airport (KPCD) gusted 56 mph and Cape Girardeau Regional Airport gusted to 61 mph. The strong winds resulted in power outages in Bollinger County and Butler County and allowed two wildfires, one southeast of Piedmont and another just northeast of Fremont, to grow rapidly out of control in the evening. Each of the fires consumed over 90 acres of the Mark Twain National Forest.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Turley 2 wildfire, located about 2 miles east northeast of Fremont in the Mark Twain National Forest, was reported by U.S. Forest Service personnel. Fanned by south southeast winds gusting 35-50mph through the evening, the fire burnt 94.5 acres before being completely extinguished. In addition to the gusty winds, response to the fire was hindered by a series of tornadic storms that swept across southeast Missouri later in the evening. A deadly EF-3 tornado ripped a path just west and north of Fremont.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper level system brought in high winds early in the day on the 14th and stuck around through the afternoon.   Breezy southwest surface winds shifted to the west with the arrival of a Pacific front. Behind this front much stronger winds aloft started to mix to the surface. Winds started gusting above 58 mph almost immediately behind the front with a ground station near Bootleg, TX measuring a gust of 59 mph at 5:10 AM CDT. The south central and southwestern TX Panhandle saw their winds peak between 1030 AM and 230 PM where some areas to the north like the OK Panhandle and to the east winds did not peak until later in the afternoon. Some of the highest winds measured were 84 mph at the mesonet station in Hereford and 83 mph measured by the Amarillo Airport ASOS around 10:43 AM CDT. These high winds quickly caused blowing dust with visibility issuse especially around the southern TX Panhandle. The high winds created problems for high profile vehicle such as tractor trailors or semi-trucks but also caused dangerous travel conditions with reduced visibilities falling below 1/4 mile. With winds being westerly this especially caused problems along I-27 south of Amarillo which runs north and south causing mutliple semi-trucks to overturn. ||Dry air which over took the Panhandles during the afternoon also combined with the high winds creating a high fire danger day. Multiple fires impacted the combined Panhandles with a couple of these fires impacting residents of around Alanreed and McLean, Texas as Fire Warnings had to be issued to prepare folks for the potential of an evacuation. One fire impacted campers at Wolf Creek Park southeast of Perryton, TX. This fire also closed down a section of HWY 70 south of Perryton.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Texas A&M Forest Service. Started on private land five miles west of Alanreed, TX. High winds caused extreme fire behavior that day.   The fire burned 7391 acres and was contained on March 16th. Cause of fire was unknown.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month of May began with overall dry conditions across the county. Green up had not occurred yet following the winter allowing fire weather conditions to increase during the first two weeks of the month. By the 11th and 12th, very warm, dry and breezy southerly winds were in place and three large fires started over those two days, the Camp House fire, the Jenkins Creek fire and the Munger Shaw fire. The fires spread quickly in those conditions and outside resources were called in to fight the fires. The Munger Shaw fire reached 1,259 acres in size and was contained on the afternoon of June 13th. The Camp House and Jenkins Creek fires were in fairly close proximity and were managed as one as the Brimson Complex. Containment for these two fires was not achieved until mid June with the Camp House reaching 12,071 acres in size and Jenkins Creek 16,490 acres. Around 150 structures were affected by the fires with most of them in the Camp House fire.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Camp House fire began on Sunday, May 11, 2025, at approximately 2PM local time in Ault Township, about two miles northeast of Brimson, Minnesota, outside the Superior National Forest. The fire was initially reported at 750 acres and expanded rapidly due to dry conditions, gusty winds, and a large volume of dead timber, particularly in areas infested with spruce budworms. It is believed to have been started by an unattended campfire. The fire moved into the Superior National Forest, causing closures and evacuations. Initial fire behavior included crown fires and rapid spread through dense forest, fueled by widespread dead and dying trees.||At least 144 structures, primarily homes and cabins along Highway 44, were destroyed by the fire's initial spread. Initially, mandatory evacuations were put in place for Highway 44 and nearby communities, and evacuation centers were established to assist displaced residents. ||On Wednesday, May 28, 2025, the the local Minnesota Department of Natural Resources (DNR) area forestry assumed management of the Camp House fire. Firefighting operations continued into June with the fire not being 100% contained until the morning of June 13th. The fire reached a maximum size of 12,071 acres and affected around 150 structures.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Munger Shaw wildfire, located approximately ten miles southeast of Cotton, Minnesota, was detected late in the afternoon on Monday, May 12. Minnesota DNR, along with local fire departments, responded. Multiple aircraft were brought in to help slow down the active flame fronts, supporting the ground firefighting efforts. The fire was active in pine and lowland fuels, but favorable weather conditions led to slow growth of the fire. The fire was believed to have started with the spontaneous combustion of a hay bale. The fire was 95% contained by Monday, May 19th, but was not fully contained until June 13th. At one point during the early days of the fire, the mainline of the Canadian National Railroad was shut down as the fire spread to both sides of the tracks. The maximum size of the fire was 1,259 acres.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Prolonged dry conditions with low relative humidity values and gusty winds allowed for multiple wildfires to begin during the afternoon of April 23, 2025 in Michaux State Forest, located in southwestern Cumberland County. The wildfire originated along Shippensburg Road between Milesburn and Thompson Road and expanded quickly in size to around 2,248 acres at the wildfire's furthest extent. At the fire's peak, aerial support was enlisted to battle the fire, along with firefighting crews on the ground. Evacuations from structures began during the afternoon hours of April 24th and continued through April 25th with 20-30 residences evacuated. While the bulk of wildfire damage was contained in April 2025, wildfires continued into early May 2025. The Thompson Hollow and Hammond Rocks wildfires caused approximately $1,100,000 in tree damage along with $800,000 in suppression costs from the beginning of the wildfires in April 2025 through the early stages of May 2025.

It was detected east of County Road 110 and north of County Road 16 near Jenkins Creek, approximately 15 miles southeast of Hoyt Lakes, Minnesota. It was believed to have been started by a discarded cigarette from a passing vehicle. The fire rapidly expanded due to hot temperatures, low relative humidity, and strong south winds, burning through mixed boreal forest and grassy ground cover, including areas heavily infested by spruce budworm, which contributed to the fire's intensity.||The fire initially exhibited extreme behavior, including crown fires and rapid spread through dense forested areas. The presence of dead and dying trees, particularly those affected by spruce budworm infestations, provided ample fuel for the fire's growth. After a couple days, the spread slowed as crews responded, winds subsided, and moisture moved into the area. Firefighters were able to take advantage of that opportunity and built a line that held through another wind event a few days later. Since then, containment continued to be effectively established with full containment achieved on June 21st. The fire reached a maximum size of 16,490 acres.

Red Flag conditions redeveloped late morning on the 20th, with strong southwest winds eventually pushing the fire into the community of Pine Valley. Washington County Sheriff reports 14 homes and 4 outbuildings destroyed in Pine Valley despite mitigation efforts. Red Flag conditions continued June 21st with the TT900 RAWS station reporting wind gusts upwards of 44 mph with RH in the single digits to teens. This resulted in the fire spreading to the north side of the valley and making a run at the communities of Grass Valley and Pinto, which were placed in an evacuation order at 5:37 PM on June 21st. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A favorable setup for strong thunderstorms over parts of the Alaska Interior and down across the Middle Kuskokwim Valley took shape during the afternoon and evening of 6/17.  Very warm temperatures in the 70s and 80s, dew points in the 50s, and a shortwave trough moving near the Alaska Range from Southcentral Alaska contributed to moderate instability and an overall environment conducive to intense thunderstorms.  Thunderstorms with frequent lighting first developed over the western Interior on the afternoon of 6/17, then moved south due to northerly steering flow into parts of the Kuskokwim Valley during the afternoon and evening hours late in the day.  The GLD lightning feed detected extremely frequent lighting with these thunderstorms, supporting convective-driven red flag conditions across much of the Middle Kuskokwim Valley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Source is global lightning (GLD) network and radar/satellite observations.  Thunderstorms producing very frequent lightning moved south between Stony River and Crooked Creek from late afternoon into the overnight on 6/17.  The frequent lightning led to significant fire weather concerns (red flag conditions due to lightning).  A staffed wildfire near Crooked Creek was alerted to the threat for thunderstorms producing frequent lighting prior to the event.

The fire was 80 percent contained by August 27th, and all evacuations and road closures were lifted. All in all, time Red Canyon fire burned nearly 125,000 acres.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper level weather system moved across the High Plains region and brought down very strong winds to the surface from the late morning to the late afternoon on February 17, 2026. Many locations across the Oklahoma Panhandle observed wind gusts o 60mph or greater. These strong winds brought blowing dust and extreme critical fire weather conditions as well. Several wildfires developed due to the dry grasses, low relative humidity and high wind gusts. One wildfire in Beaver County burned into Kansas and consumed over 200,000 acres.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Ranger Road fire ignited during the morning of February 17th near Highway 64, one mile southeast of Beaver, Oklahoma. This fire burned 283,283 acres across Oklahoma and Kansas. The fire was fueled by dormant, dry grasses and brush, driven by wind gusts of 60-70 mph and extremely low humidity (10-15%). These conditions created a fast fire environment, allowing the blaze to explode in size���growing from ignition to 15,000 acres in one hour to over 145,000 acres in just nine hours. It rapidly crossed the state line into Clark, Comanche, and Meade counties in Kansas. With strong wind gusts, this helped not only to spread the fire but limited aerial firefighting operations and complicated suppression efforts during the first stages of the fire's expansion. The cause is undetermined.  A firefighter was injured from being burned. In addition, a fire truck from Rosston Fire overturned in Beaver County and three fire fighters were injured, including one that suffered from 2nd and 3rd degree burns and broke his leg. There were 926 primary homes, 2 schools, and commercial/government buildings threatened. Evacuations: Mandatory evacuations for about 771 people that may have covered KS as well.  Gate and Knowles had evacuations on Feb 17th, and numerous outbuildings were destroyed in the fire.

The fire burned 12,894 acres and was caused by human activities. Smoke from this fire reduced visibility along US Highway 54, which resulted in a seven vehicle accident and additional fire start(which became the Side Road Fire). Mandatory evacuations occurred for the town of Tyrone on the 17th and were lifted by the morning of February 21st. US Highway 54 was closed between Tyrone and Hooker due to smoke and fire activity.  Five structures were burned: 4 barns and one house per OEMA. About 263 homes were threatened by this fire.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper level weather system moved across the High Plains region and brought down very strong winds to the surface from the late morning to the late afternoon on February 17, 2026. A wide array of high winds in the 60 mph range affected the majority of the Texas Panhandle and some locations even experienced wind gusts over 70 mph. Damage to homes, structures, and overturned semi-trucks occurred during the afternoon as a result of these stronger winds. Blowing dust and extreme critical fire weather conditions were also present thanks to the strong winds and several wildfires occurred across the Texas Panhandle as a result.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Lavender Fire ignited on February 17, 2026, approximately five miles south of Boys Ranch in Oldham County. The fire began along the U.S. Highway 385 corridor. The fire was fueled by critically dry, waist-high grass and extreme wind conditions. It exhibited rapid growth initially, pushed by strong west winds with gusts reaching 50-60 mph. The fire quickly crossed key roadways, including FM 1061 (Tascosa Road), and spread toward the Canadian River. In total, the Lavender Fire burned 18423 acres across Oldham County and into Potter County.  Mandatory evacuations were issued for the Valley De Oro community and areas between Tascosa Road (FM 1061) and U.S. Highway 287 in north-central Potter County during the afternoon of February 17th. The Ady neighborhood was also evacuated on February 18th. FM 1061(Tascosa Road) at US Highway 385/281 was closed due to fires during the afternoon of February 17th and was reopened during the evening of February 18th. The Texas Department of Public Safety also shutdown Highway 287 on February 17th and US 87 was closed in both directions from FM 1719, just north of Amarillo to SH 354, south of Dumas. Approximately 250 people and homes were affected.  Incident report noted 40 homes saved, and 7 homes lost. In addition, Xcel Energy implemented a Public Safety Power Shutoff (PSPS) to reduce wildfire risk, which affected thousands of customers and resulted in some schools closing for the day due to lack of electricity and ability to feed students. The cause of the fire is undetermined.

It exhibited rapid growth initially, spreading from a reported 200 acres to thousands of acres within the first 24 hours. Forward progress of the fire was stopped on the evening of February 18th but was contained on February 21st. In total, Eight Ball Fire burned 13563 acres across Armstrong and Donley counties.  There were evacuations in the Howardwick area on February 17th, which were lifted later on February 18th. US Highway 287 was closed from Goodnight to Ashtola for a couple of hours. Highway 70 was also briefly closed. The fire threatened approximately 1,100 homes and critical infrastructure. At the peak of the event, roughly 400 homes were evacuated.  The cause of the fire is human related with a connection to passenger vehicle or motorized RV usage.

The final size of the fire was 6,949 acres. The cause of the fire was unknown. Cabin Creek Fire. The cause of the fire is believed to be human, from a passenger vehicle. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong backdoor front moved south and west across eastern New Mexico late March 26th into early March 27th resulting in strong north winds at several locations. The strong northerly winds aided the rapid spread of the Old 66 Wildfire that began just north of I-40 near San Jon, jumping south of the highway. This fire destroyed two structures, but did not cause any injuries or loss of life. The cold front surged through the gaps of the central mountain chain just before sunrise resulting in strong to high east canyon winds across the Tularosa Valley and middle and lower Rio Grande Valley. Mesonet sites across White Sands Missile Range measured wind gusts up to 93 mph. Winds across eastern New Mexico tapered off during the late morning hours while winds across the Tularosa and Rio Grande Valley tapered off during the mid to late evening hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Old 66 Wildfire was discovered mid-day March 27th, and quickly grew out of control north of I-40 near San Jon, NM. It burned quickly southward through grasslands crossing I-40 aided by strong northerly to northeasterly winds behind a strong cold front, growing to a final size of 4,111 acres. The fire came under control as winds subsided heading into March 28th. The fire caused a closure of NM 469 and Main Ave. in San Jon, NM. Emergency management reported the fire destroyed two structures, and that a wind farm that was threatened did not suffer any damage. No injuries or loss of life was reported. Damage is an estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: With very little winter precipitation that occurred across the combined Panhandles, and little to no significant precipitation continuing through the early Spring, critical fire weather conditions prevailed for much of the month. Many days in March were characterized by either low relative humidity values in the single digits or days with winds of around 40-50mph, or both. With very dry, freeze cured fuels, this combination allowed for prolonged higher fire danger and multiple wildfires across the Panhandles. Most were human caused, but some were started from dry lightning in the few thunderstorms that did occur during the month.

The South Dakota Department of Transportation (SDDOT) Road Weather Information System (RWIS) 1 mile west northwest of Summit recorded a wind gust as high as 79 mph, while the SDDOT RWIS 3 miles southeast of Reliance recorded a peak wind of 77 mph. Another 23 weather stations would record a peak wind in excess of 70 mph. ||These high winds were responsible for at least one semi being blown off Interstate 29 near Summit, forcing a closure of the southbound lane.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Cooperative Institute for Meteorological Satellite Studies (CIMSS) fire detection tool identified a hot spot northeast of the community of Green Grass in the early afternoon of March 12th. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Unified Wildfire began in the morning of March 24th in the bosque area along the Rio Grande just southeast of Belen near the small town of Madrone, NM. EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Emergency Manager reported the start of the Unified Fire within the bosque area of the Rio Grande just southeast of Belen near the town of Madrone, NM. The fire quickly grew out of control in very dry and receptive fuels in the area thanks to persistent by modest southeasterly winds. Evacuations were ordered along Lagrima Road and Madrone Flyway road. Winds lessened during the evening of March 24th into the morning of March 25th as the fire grew to 300 total acres. The fire came under control March 25th with mop-up activities continuing a few days afterward. No damage to any structures, injuries, or fatalities were reported from this fire.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Fire initiated southeast of Angora Nebraska in eastern Morrill County during the afternoon hours of March 12th.  Aided by west-northwest winds, gusting over 50 MPH, fire raced to the east-southeast. By late evening on March 12th, the fire had tracked some 70 miles across Garden County into southwestern Arthur, far southwestern Grant, and northwestern Keith County. By the time the fire was contained on March 28th, 642,029 acres were consumed.  The Morrill fire was the largest fire on record in the state of Nebraska. One direct fatality occurred as a result of the fire.

By the time the fire was contained on March 28th, approximately 64,590 acres of rangeland was consumed in the fire. The fire resulted in one fatality in southwestern Arthur County. One primary residence was destroyed, along with 6 outbuildings damaged in the fire. Two calf-cow pairs were lost in the fire in Arthur County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level system brought showers and thunderstorms during the late afternoon and evening of March 10th across the combined Panhandles. The thunderstorms impacted the northeast but the state of the atmosphere was conducive for strong winds aloft to come down to the surface with even some of the lighter showers and storms. This created a few wind gusts exceeding 58 mph. The next morning, on the 11th, the upper level system brought high winds to the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles which created wind gusts upwards of 71 mph early in the morning hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: On March 10th, a high based thunderstorm with dry lightning ignited a wildfire in far southwest Moore County. The fire, which would be named Yellow Fire, sparked around 6:30pm and occurred near the border of Moore, Oldham and Hartley counties. Gusty, erratic winds occurred at the Boys Ranch mesonet around that time, and while relative humidity values were around 20%, the winds and the critically dry fuels allowed for rapid wildfire growth. The wildfire was estimated to have burned 14,374 acres and was contained on March 13th. East and westbound SH 354 was temporarily closed from US Highway 385 to US Highway 87 from March 10th through early on the 11th. Additional roads also experienced at least temporary closures such as RM 1061 at FM 281 and Highway 385. There was also a voluntary evacuation of Valley de Oro and an evacuation of the Boys Ranch community.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme to exceptional drought continued or worsened for the majority of the region throughout the month of April. This, combined with many days of breezy to gusty wind conditions, resulted in a number of wildfires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Sargent wildfire  developed in northwest Baker county, northern Osceola National Forest on April 2, 2026 around 350 PM EDT. The smoke plume extended northward affecting local roads near the Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge and into Waycross, GA. On April 3rd, the Florida Forest Service reported the Sargent Fire quickly grew to about 4,000 acres moving into Columbia and Clinch counties. The highway between Fargo, GA and John Bethea State Forest in Florida was closed (Highway 2 in Florida and Highway 94 in Georgia). The majority of the fire was burning in Florida but it had crossed into southern Georgia. On the evening of April 3rd, the fire was now estimated at 2,720 acres and 50% contained following improved mapping. On April 5th, Florida Highway 2 and Georgia Highway 94 were now only closed at night due to potential low visibility from fog and smoke. Light rain on April 5th and 6th was not enough to help put out the fire. On April 11th, the fire was 81% contained at 2,489 acres. On April 15th, reburn in the swamp occurred due to hot and dry weather. On April 20th, the acreage increased to 2,523 acres due to spotfires which are caused by flying sparks or embers carried by the wind from an existing fire and ignite a new fire. No structures were threatened. Breezy winds, extreme to exceptional drought conditions, lack of beneficial rain, and remaining heavy fuels continued elevated fire activity through the month of April.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On April 20, 2026 at 4 PM EDT, the Georgia Forestry Commission reported a wildfire developed along Highway 82 near Atkinson, GA. The Highway 82 fire was caused by a Mylar balloon coming into contact with a power line, creating an electrical arc that ignited the surrounding vegetation. This wildfire resulted in the worst home loss from a single fire in Georgia history. The wildfire was difficult to contain because of hot and dry conditions, extended long-term drought, breezy winds and lack of rain across southeast Georgia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: On April 20, 2026 at 4 PM EDT, the Georgia Forestry Commission reported a wildfire developed along Highway 82 near Atkinson, GA. The Highway 82 fire was caused by a Mylar balloon coming into contact with a power line, creating an electrical arc that ignited the surrounding vegetation. This wildfire resulted in the worst home loss from a single fire in Georgia history, with 110 homes destroyed and 27 homes damaged. On April 25th, the fire grew to 9,578 acres per overnight infrared flight mapping. The winds shifted to southwesterly pushing smoke from Brantley County to Glynn County, with heavy smoke around Post Road and Highway 32. The fire was 13,745 acres and 7% contained. The fire produced 150-foot flame lengths during a significant run toward Browntown Road. The blaze was a plume-dominated wildfire, a rare occurrence that happened on multiple days during the fire. On April 26th, Glynn County EM issued Mandatory Evacuations for Old Post Road to Highway 32, Highway 32 to Thalman Park Lane, Thalman Park Lane to Bladen Road and Bladen Road to Old Post Road. Infrared mapping showed the fire at approximately 20,933 acres with 7% containment. Without precipitation, the fire was very active again with wind driven movement to the northeast and east until the wind shifted in the afternoon with the sea breeze. At 8 PM, an isolated thunderstorm moved over the fire bringing rain amounts of 0.4 to 0.8 inches. This amount of rain did not extinguish the fire, but briefly decreased the extreme fire behavior. On April 27th, winds shifted to north-northeasterly which led to Glynn county downgrading evacuations and re-opening previously closed roads. On April 28th, the fire was 22,600 acres and 32% contained. On April 30th, roads from Browntown south of Murphy Road and HWY 32 were opened. The fire was 22,532 acres and 37% contained. More smoke occurred on April 30th in bay vegetation due to hot and dry conditions, extended long-term drought and lack of rain.

Mandatory evacuations continued into the evening and were issued for Happy Hollow, Drury Ln, Drury Ct, Coffee County Club Rd and From Thrower Rd to Mossy Oak as the fire grew quickly to 5,000 acres. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month of April ended with well above normal precipitation but that quickly transitioned to very dry conditions in May with rainfall amounts only around 5-20% of normal over the first half of the month. Some locations in the Brainerd Lakes area to near Grand Rapids received little, if any precipitation during this time. With green up yet to occur, fuels quickly dried out across the region. May 15th saw a deep low pressure system pass by well to the north setting up westerly to southwesterly winds gusting to 30 to 40 mph the 15th and 16th with very dry conditions lead to Red Flag Warnings across the Northland. Multiple fires began over those two days with two fires, the Flanders Fire and the Stewart Trail Fire becoming quite large and leading to evacuations. The fires spread quickly in those conditions and outside resources were called in to fight the fires. The Flanders Fire reached 1,685 acres in size and was contained on the afternoon of the 20th. The Stewart Trail fire near Two Harbors reached 375 acres in size and destroyed over 30 structures, including homes and cabins along Lake Superior.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Stewart Trail Fire began on Friday, May 15th around 2PM local time near Stewart Trail off County Highway 3 just north of Minnesota Highway 61 in Two Harbors. Very dry and windy conditions were in place with westerly winds gusting to 30 to 40 mph during the early afternoon with relative humidity values falling below 30%, creating dangerous fire weather conditions across the region. The fire was started by a downed power line from the winds and quickly spread to Highway 61 and then up the North Shore to near Castle Danger. Within an hour of the fire starting, structures were being impacted along Highway 61 and the fire was torching in the trees with flames 50 to 60 feet in length in addition to spotting. Highway 61 was quickly closed and evacuations began. Favorable weather conditions, including cooler temperatures, higher humidity, and rainfall, aided firefighters over the weekend allowing the fire to be contained by late afternoon on Monday the 18th. Over 30 structures, including homes and cabins, were destroyed by the fire. The fire reached a maximum size of 375 acres.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme to exceptional drought, dry fuels, and breezy days triggered numerous wildfires in southeast Georgia and northeast Florida in April that continued through the month of May. EVENT_NARRATIVE: On April 20, 2026 at 4 PM EDT, the Georgia Forestry Commission reported a wildfire developed along Highway 82 near Atkinson, GA. The Highway 82 fire was caused by a Mylar balloon coming into contact with a power line, creating an electrical arc that ignited the surrounding vegetation. This wildfire resulted in the worst home loss from a single fire in Georgia history, with 110 homes destroyed and 27 homes damaged. On May 1st, the fire was 22,532 acres and 45% contained. Boots Harrison Road, North of Albert Gibson Road and Highway 32 from US 301 to Highway 99 remained closed due to fire and smoke. At 7 PM, the Georgia Department of Transportation (DOT) reopened SR 110 to traffic in Brantley County. On May 2nd, Hwy 32 was opened from US 301 to 110w and from Post Road to Browntown Road. About an inch of rain fell on the wildfire on May 2nd which helped reduce fire activity and helped crews increase the containment to 64%. On May 3rd, evacuation orders impacting residences were lifted for Brantley county. All roads reopened except for Highway 32. The fire was 22,471 acres and 75% contained, per the National Interagency Fire Center (NIFC). On May 4th, the fire was 22,420 acres and 85% contained. On May 7th, Hwy 32 reopened and the fire was 90% contained. Crews observed reburn within the fire interior near State Route 110 and Stewart Road, State Route 110 and Dogwood Road, and Browntown Road due to strong winds across the area. On May 9th, steady rainfall over the fire area throughout the day helped reduce fire activity across much of the incident. On May 29th, the fire was 95% contained, per the NIFC. One minor injury occurred among more than 600 personnel.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A prolonged hot and dry period was set up for the Panhandles in mid May.  And with the lack of significant rainfall to help transition the grasses from cured to green, the fuels were well above the 90th percentile in dryness. Several lightning ignitions occurred, and given that the storms had severe dry microbursts associated, the fires that ignited would spread quickly.  Thereafter the Panhandles would go through several consecutive days of critical to extremely critical conditions.  And the issues of any new starts, as well as active fires that ignited on May 14th would take another run were of high concern. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level disturbance moving across the central Rockies combined with higher moisture across the southeast plains of NM resulted in the development of multiple severe thunderstorms across southern Roosevelt County during the mid afternoon to mid evening hours. These thunderstorms resulted in three rounds of hail up to ping pong diameter between Pep and the Roosevelt and Lea County border. Back building of severe thunderstorms across this area resulted in some minor flooding in culverts and low lying areas. Thunderstorms tapered off just before sunset on May 21st due to the loss of daytime heating. Two more rounds of thunderstorms developed across the northeast and east central plains of NM during the afternoon on May 22nd and 23rd. These storms resulted in a severe wind gust at a public weather station near Melrose on May 22nd and at Tucumcari Municipal Airport on May 23rd. Storms exited into west Texas during the evening hours. The Trigg wildfire was also discovered in far eastern San Miguel County, burning through May 25th before coming under control.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At around 11:30 AM MST on the 11th, a new wildfire named the Jones Fire broke out just southeast of Downtown Wickenburg along a riverbed near a Ford Dealership. The fire was able to spread along a riverbed, jumping U.S. Highway 60 (the main highway corridor connecting Phoenix and Las Vegas). The fire was able to be fully contained approximately 100 hours after its initial start with a total of 84 acres burned. The fire caused the closure of U.S. Highway 60 for a period and destroyed several structures and vehicles nearby with approximately 25 people displaced. Very hot and dry conditions with temperatures near 100 degrees along with very light winds were observed around the time the fire ignited. No injuries were reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A new wildfire named the Jones Fire broke out just southeast of Downtown Wickenburg along a riverbed near a Ford Dealership. The fire was able to spread along the riverbed, jumping U.S. Highway 60 (the main highway corridor connecting Phoenix and Las Vegas) and forcing its closure. At the end, the blaze destroyed approximately eleven RVs, seven vehicles, two trailers, and two outbuildings with 25 people displaced. The fire also damaged some electrical equipment causing a power outage with approximately 176 customers affected. In total, the fire consumed nearly 84 acres. No injuries were reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extremely critical fire weather conditions highlighted by peak wind gusts of 55 to 70 mph alongside humidity ranging from 15 to 25 percent were present February 17th. This allowed for the Smith Wildfire to quickly grow out of control in Harding County approximately 3 miles northeast of Mosquero. Southwest winds combined with the location of the fire northeast of Mosquero allowed there to be no damage or evacuations resulting from this fire. It's growth subsided considerably after winds waned during the 20th to 22nd.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Smith Wildfire ignited Tuesday, February 17th during extremely critical fire weather conditions. Strong southwest winds allowed it to quickly grow, but thankfully its location northeast of Mosquero allowed it to grow away from town. There were no known evacuation orders or damage from this fire as it eventually grew to 3,797 acres before waning February 22nd as winds subsided.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful upper level storm system that spread eastward from the Intermountain West brought widespread high winds, blowing dust, and a few wildfires on the morning and afternoon of the 17th. Thick high level cloud cover early in the day initially prevented strong winds from developing. However, these clouds began to thin out and clear by late in the morning from west to east. This allowed surface winds to quickly ramp up where clearing occurred. Most observed severe wind gusts were between 58 and 65 mph, however, the Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Olton measured a wind gust of 77 mph. These strong winds also lofted copious amounts of dust into the atmosphere which reduced visibility across the South Plains and extreme southern Texas Panhandle.
